The papers don't give a maximum Poisson's ratio specifically for V₂O₅. The only discussion is in the ACS Nano paper (acsnano-7b02404):

- **General range for oxides:** The authors note that "most oxides have a Poisson coefficient 'v' between 0 and 0.5." This is a general statement about oxides, not a measured value for V₂O₅ (page 3).
- **Value they used:** They "assumed a Poisson coefficient v = 0.3 (typical for metal oxides)" to estimate in-plane strain. On that basis, a 0.5% out-of-plane compressive strain along 'c' corresponds to about 1.6% in-plane tensile strain (page 3). They repeat the assumption ("assuming ~0.3 in our case") when explaining the net volume increase of the strained film (page 6).

So 0.5 is the upper bound the paper cites for oxides in general, and 0.3 is an assumed value rather than a measured property of their V₂O₅ films. None of the other attached papers give a Poisson's ratio for V₂O₅.
